title: Mock: Full Loop, Then Close the Cycle
focus: Three back-to-back rounds the way an onsite actually runs, then the review that decides what next month looks like.

cards.title: Round A: Two Mediums, 45 Minutes
cards.trigger: Two problems in one slot is the most common Google format. Pacing is the skill being tested.
cards.recall: Set forty-five minutes for both. Budget twenty for the first. If the first runs over, you must consciously decide to move on. That decision is the exercise.
template: # Two-problem pacing:
#   the interviewer has a second problem queued and wants to reach it
#   finishing one perfectly and never seeing the second scores WORSE
#   than solid work on both
# So at the halfway mark, if you are not close, say:
#   'I want to make sure we get to the second problem. Shall I finish
#    this one, or move on and come back if there is time?'
# That sentence is a senior signal. It shows you are managing the session,
# not just the problem.
keyInsights: Pacing is graded, silently. Running out of time on problem one is a common and avoidable failure
Asking to move on hands the decision back to the interviewer, which is exactly right, and costs you nothing
The easy problem in a two-problem slot is a warm-up. Spending fifteen minutes on it is the actual mistake
cards.trap: Optimising problem one from O(n log n) to O(n) while problem two sits untouched. Good enough, then move, is the correct strategy.

cards.title: Round B: One Hard, 45 Minutes
cards.trigger: The differentiating round. Hards are usually a medium plus one insight.
cards.recall: Pick a hard you have not touched in two weeks. Before starting, write down which medium it resembles and what the extra insight probably is. Then check yourself against the real solution.
template: # The 'which medium is this' reduction, for the five above:
#   serialize     -> tree DFS, plus null markers to fix ambiguity
#   merge k       -> merge two, plus a heap to pick the smallest head
#   burst         -> interval DP, plus the LAST-move reframing
#   word ladder   -> BFS, plus the graph is computed rather than stored
#   first missing -> cyclic sort, plus the 1..n+1 bound
# Every hard in this program reduces this way. Find the reduction and
# you have found the solution.
keyInsights: Naming the underlying medium is faster and more reliable than trying to derive a hard from scratch
The 'extra insight' is usually a reframing, not extra code. Last-move, inverted search, implicit graph
If forty-five minutes pass with no insight, the brute force plus a clear statement of what is missing is a genuine partial pass
cards.trap: Treating hards as a separate category to be memorised. They are compositions. Learn the reductions, not the solutions.

cards.title: Round C: Design and Complexity, 45 Minutes
cards.trigger: Build a data structure to a stated complexity contract, then defend every choice.
cards.recall: Pick one. Before coding, write the operation table: every method, its required complexity, and which structure provides it. Then build. Then defend each choice as if challenged.
template: # The operation table. Write it BEFORE any code.
#   method        required      structure providing it
#   get(k)        O(1)          hash map
#   put(k, v)     O(1)          hash map + list splice
#   evict()       O(1)          doubly linked list tail
# Then the three questions they will ask:
#   'What happens at capacity zero?'
#   'What is the memory overhead per entry?'
#   'How would you make it thread safe / distributed?'
keyInsights: The operation table forces the design before the syntax, and it is what the interviewer is actually evaluating
Memory overhead per entry is a real question at Google scale, and almost nobody has an answer ready
Thread safety is usually 'a lock around the whole thing, then shard by key hash to reduce contention'. Have that sentence
cards.trap: Answering 'how would you scale this' with vague distributed-systems words. Say sharding by key hash, say what breaks (global LRU ordering), and say the trade you would accept.

cards.title: Weak Spot Sweep
cards.trigger: Thirty minutes on the concepts still marked shaky. This is the highest-value half hour of the entire month.
cards.recall: Open the weak-spots list. For every concept still marked shaky, write its template from memory right now. The ones that fail are the ones that start next month.
template: # What 'shaky' actually costs you:
#   a shaky concept is not a concept you might get wrong.
#   it is a concept you will spend eight minutes rediscovering,
#   in a twenty-five minute round, while the clock runs.
# The rule for next month:
#   shaky twice  -> write it out three times on paper this week
#   shaky three times -> the underlying idea is missing, not the code.
#                        Go back and learn the idea, not the template.
# Everything solid twice in a row is safe to run at speed next cycle.
keyInsights: Spaced repetition only works if the weak items actually resurface. That is what the shaky marking is for
Three failures on the same concept means you are memorising code without the idea. Stop drilling and go learn it
The list should shrink every month. If it does not, you are running the cycle without acting on it
cards.trap: Marking things solid because you recognised them. Recognition is not recall. If your pen did not move, it is shaky.

cards.title: Close the Cycle
cards.trigger: Cycle complete. 150 problems, 150 concept touches. Now decide what the next one looks like.
cards.recall: Write the four answers below. Then start Day 1 tomorrow, and notice how much faster it goes than it did this month.
template: # Four questions, in writing:
#   1. Which lane was slowest this cycle? (arrays / design / trees / dp / graphs)
#   2. How many concepts are still shaky, and is that fewer than last month?
#   3. What was my average clean-recall rate, and did the combo streaks get longer?
#   4. What is the ONE process fix carried into next cycle?
# Then reset and run it again. Same 30 days, same 150 problems.
# Cycle 1: you are learning the patterns.
# Cycle 2: you are recognising them.
# Cycle 3: you are writing them without thinking.
# Cycle 4: the interview is a formality.
# The repetition IS the method. Do not swap in new problems because
# these feel familiar. Familiar is the entire objective.
keyInsights: Same content every month is the design, not a limitation. Novelty feels productive and builds nothing durable
The metric that matters is clean-recall rate, not problems solved. Solved-while-peeking is a lookup, not a memory
By cycle three the templates should come out faster than you can read the problem statement
cards.trap: Getting bored and swapping in a fresh problem set. That resets you to cycle one on every pattern, and boredom is the feeling of something becoming automatic.
